Palette samples

Two sets of samples, each built on the real homepage skeleton — same markup, same type, same layout. Nothing here is live; production stays untouched until a winner is picked.

Set 1 — The Study, dark. The current palette first, as a control, then three candidates. All four wear the settled blue chrome (nav, kickers, the In Brief heading), so the only thing on trial is the palette itself.

Set 2 — The Board, light. The current cream first, then three steps toward a cleaner paper. Ink and red never move — only the ground’s warmth, and the tint, rule, gray and nav companions it drags with it.

THE STUDY

The latest
session

Saturday, November 21, 2026

The Gospel of Mark

The earliest Gospel, read slowly and honestly: who wrote it, when, what in it can be checked, and why it still sets the terms for everything written after.

This session takes up the Gospel of Mark, the earliest of the four and the shortest. It was written about forty years after the crucifixion, most likely near the year 70, by an author who never names himself and never claims to have seen the events he describes.

Mark is also where this study has to begin, because of how the book ends, and because its ending is not the one most readers think they know. The case for the resurrection starts here, and it starts in silence.

In Brief

What does the text actually say? Who wrote it, and when? What in it can be checked against the evidence?

What did it mean to the people who heard it first? What pattern runs underneath the story? And what did its values go on to build?

Control — Current Umber

What is live on The Study now: deep umber ground, vellum ink, oxblood and gold accents — shown here with the settled blue chrome in place of the oxblood, so the palette alone is being judged. Oxblood #c05f4d and aged gold #a07d2c are the current accents this scheme would retire from chrome.

Candidate A — Radix Umber

Built on the Radix Brown dark scale, the research’s warm model: page #12110F, subtle surface #1C1816 (the nav), callout #28211D (the In Brief block). The warmth is a whisper — you cannot name this ground as brown, which is exactly where the current #221b14 fails. Ink is parchment #F2E1CA, softened a step for body text; hairlines are translucent warm white (the rule chip shows the blend over the ground). Oxblood is gone from the page; parchment-gold and a light claret survive only as accent options inside divider motifs.

Candidate C — Slate

The same darkness floor, cooled to an ink-blue slate so the royal blue is native to the page instead of applied to it. The blue is lifted to the light register the research requires on dark grounds — the saturated version measures under 3:1 and vibrates. Warm vellum ink keeps the manuscript contrast. Oxblood is dropped; gold is kept only inside divider motifs.

THE BOARD

The latest
report

Friday, November 20, 2026

The Power of the People

The whole history of ordinary people against the people who ruled them, from the first farming towns to today.

Did ordinary people ever take power from the people who ruled them? For most of history, no. Rulers held it, everyone else lived under it, and every challenge died with the people who made it. Then, after 1800, it happened once, in one domain, and it has not been repeated.

The domain was formal political status: the vote, legal equality, national sovereignty, now held by billions of people whose ancestors held none of them. The rest of the record, the long stretch where rulers seem to be losing, sorts three ways. Sometimes the loss was real. Sometimes it was a loan, recalled within weeks. And very often it was a change of costume, from a lord you could petition or flee to a system you cannot argue with.

Read the full report →

The Power of the People · Evening Report

Inside the report

The grain machine.Writing began as accounting: wedges in wet clay recording barley, beer, and rations owed. The grain state made refusal expensive, and Athens shows both halves of the exception, depth inside a fence of citizens who were 10 to 20 percent of the population.Go to The Grain Machine → The great concession.After 1800 the vote, legal equality, and sovereignty moved to billions, priced by war, taxation, and threat. Wealth did not move with them: the richest tenth owns 76 percent of it, and union membership has fallen from about 35 percent to 9.9.Go to The Great Concession →

The Board’s current paper, exactly as published. Ink #141310 and red #b03a2e are held constant across all four light samples.
